15 Key Stats to Know Before Betting on the Week 7 NFL Slate 🏈

1. The Colts will be without superstar cornerback Sauce Gardner this week, which sets up Justin Jefferson to dominate in this matchup. With Gardner out, I’m expecting the Colts defense to lean more heavily into Cover 2 and Cover 3. Against those coverages this season, Jefferson is averaging 3.47 YPRR with a 0.37 TPRR. Additionally, the Colts’ passing defense hasn’t been great this season, ranking 21st in EPA (0.02) and 20th in success rate (44.7%). As Kyler Murray gets more familiar with KOC’s scheme, I’m expecting the Vikings’ passing offense to continue improving.

2. Chuba Hubbard draws a tough matchup this week against a Bucs rush defense that has been excellent this year. Through six games, the Bucs rush defense ranks 3rd in EPA allowed (-0.19), 5th in success rate (36.8%), and 2nd in YPC allowed (3.49). Now let’s look at how the Bucs defend zone concepts. Against zone concepts this season, they are allowing 4.03 YPC with a 45.9% success rate. That’s significant because 62.9% of Hubbard’s rushes this season have come on zone concepts. Additionally, the Bucs have used a heavy box on 31.5% of their defensive snaps. I don’t expect Hubbard to have much success on the ground in this matchup.

3. Chris Olave gets a sneaky matchup this week against a Steelers defense that has run a ton of Cover 3/4 (60.7% rate) over the past month. Against Cover 3/4 this season, Olave is averaging 3.16 YPRR with a 0.34 TPRR. He also owns a 40.8% first-read share against those coverages.

4. Woody Marks is set to have himself a day against a Giants rush defense that has been atrocious this season. Through six games, the Giants rush defense rank 29th in EPA allowed (0.00), 26th in success rate (44.1%), 31st in YPC allowed (5.05), and 24th in stuff rate (18.4%). Additionally, the Giants have really struggled against man/gap concepts, allowing 4.98 YPC and a 52.5% success rate on those rushes. That’s significant because 62.1% of Marks’ rushes this year have come on man/gap concepts. With the Texans favored by 10.5 points, Marks should also get a favorable game script.

5. The Raiders defense has really struggled to stop the run this year when teams are in 13 personnel. Opponents are averaging 5.32 YPC against the Raiders out of 13 personnel, and the Raiders own just a 32.1% success rate when defending those rushes. That’s significant because the Rams are running 13 personnel at the highest rate in the league (31%). With Davante Adams out and Puka Nacua questionable with a calf injury, I’m expecting the Rams to lean heavily on 13 personnel. That sets up Kyren Williams for a big day—he’s averaging 5.33 YPC this year out of 13 personnel. In a game the Rams desperately need a win, I expect Sean McVay to lean on his ground game.

6. Carnell Tate is set up for success against a Browns defense that has run 1-high looks at a 75.8% rate over the past month. Tate is averaging 2.32 YPRR with a 0.29 TPRR against Cover 1/3 this year. With the Titans’ run game likely to struggle, I expect Tate to cook. (The Browns are also getting Mason Graham back, which should help their run defense.)

7. Tucker Kraft gets an excellent matchup this week against a Lions defense that is allowing the most receiving yards to opposing tight ends in the league. Over the past month, the Lions have run Cover 1/3 at a 59.5% rate. Against 1-high looks this year, Kraft is averaging 1.61 YPRR with a 0.24 TPRR. With the Lions’ passing defense ranking 29th in success rate (49.4%) and 29th in EPA (0.20), I expect Kraft to cook on National Tight Ends Day. The Lions do get star safety Brian Branch back, but Branch isn’t going to line up against Kraft.

8. The Falcons are allowing the third-most targets to opposing running backs this season, which sets Christian McCaffrey up to dominate this spot. With Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel out, McCaffrey should lead the 49ers pass-catchers in targets. Over the past month, the Falcons have primarily operated in Cover 1/3/4 (83.1% rate). Against those coverages, CMC is averaging 0.21 TPRR. In a game where the 49ers’ offense might struggle to move the ball, he should be Brock Purdy’s safety valve.

9. Malik Washington gets a sneaky matchup this week against a Jets defense that has run a ton of Cover 1/2 over the past month (41.7% rate). Against those coverages, Washington is averaging 2.0 YPRR with a 0.47 TPRR. Additionally, Jarvis Brownlee Jr. is expected to shadow him, and Brownlee has struggled in coverage this year (104.4 passer rating allowed when targeted). In a likely trailing game script, Washington should see a decent amount of targets.

10. The Bengals’ rush defense has struggled in one specific area this season: allowing explosive runs. Through six weeks, they are allowing an 18.8% explosive run rate and have given up 371 yards on those runs. That’s significant because Derrick Henry owns a 13% explosive run rate this year and has already gained 213 yards on those runs.

11. Jaylen Warren is set up for success against a Saints defense that has struggled against the run. Through six games, the Saints rank 31st in success rate (47.4%), 32nd in EPA (0.04), and 28th in YPC allowed (4.79). They have also really struggled against man/gap concepts, allowing 5.06 YPC with a 62.3% success rate. Warren is averaging 5.26 YPC on man/gap rushes this year.

12. Mike Macdonald’s defense has done an excellent job limiting pass explosives this season. Through six games, the Seahawks rank 2nd in EPA per pass (-0.19) and 1st in YPA allowed (5.23). Xavier Worthy looks like the Chiefs pass-catcher most likely to struggle—he owns just a 4.14 aDOT and is averaging only 1.5 YPRR against Cover 4/6 this year. That’s relevant because the Seahawks have run Cover 4/6 at a 47.1% rate over the past month. With the Seahawks allowing the fewest receiving yards to opposing wide receivers, I don’t expect Worthy to have much success.

13. If Patrick Surtain is unable to play this week, Michael Wilson is set to have himself a day. Against Cover 1/3/6 this year, Wilson is averaging 1.6 YPRR with a 0.28 TPRR and owns a 32.6% first-read share against those coverages. In a favorable game script, he should thrive if Surtain is out.

14. Jonathan Taylor gets a difficult matchup this week against a Vikings defense that has been excellent against the run. Through six weeks, the Vikings rank 2nd in success rate (33.3%), 8th in EPA (-0.16), and 6th in YAC per attempt allowed (0.85). What makes the Vikings rush defense so good is that they blitz at the highest rate in the league (66.7%). Against zone concepts, Brian Flores’ defense is allowing just 2.97 YPC with a 36.4% success rate. Nearly 60% of Taylor’s rushes this year have come on zone concepts. In a likely trailing game script, I expect the Colts to lean more on Daniel Jones’ arm in this game.

15. After 673 days, Tank Dell is back, and I really like an angle for him in this matchup against the Giants. I expect him to get a designed target, especially with his entire family in attendance. Dell himself said: “I don’t care if the first catch is two yards, five yards, I’m spiking a ball, I’m doing what I got to do. It’s going to feel good. I know there’s a lot of questions like, ‘How is he going to look when he gets tackled?’ I don’t care about any of that. I’m ready to get tackled. I’m going to be joyful. You all are going to see the passion I have after I have that first catch.” Additionally, through 6 games the Giants defense has allowed 59 targets to the slot. Regardless, as a fan of the sport, I’m glad to see Tank Dell back from that gruesome injury.

Thanks for reading my Week 7 notes ❤️

🚨 FOOTBALL MANAGER 27 CHALLENGES UNTIL I HIT THE CHARACTER LIMIT 🚨

1) European ladder Challenge - Start in Tier 7 and climb seven tiers of European leagues ranked by UEFA coefficient. You can only move up after winning your current tier’s league title, and only manage clubs from countries that have never won the European Cup/Champions League. The ultimate goal is to win a Tier 1 league and the Champions League, with an exception to the country rule for the final tier.

2) The Pentagon Challenge - Start unemployed with no coaching badges or playing experience and work your way around the world, winning all five continental club competitions: the UEFA Champions League, Copa Libertadores, AFC Champions League Elite, CAF Champions League and CONCACAF Champions Cup.

3) Moneyball Challenge - Take charge of a club and build a winning team using only data to identify signings. You can only sign players based on their performance statistics, without using attributes, star ratings or scout recommendations. The ultimate goal is to win major trophies by finding undervalued players through data alone.

4) Sir Alex Ferguson Challenge - Holiday until 6 November and take charge of the club sitting 19th in the Premier League. Stay there for 27 seasons, aiming to replicate Sir Alex Ferguson's achievements: win the FA Cup within four seasons, Premier League within seven, domestic double within eight and treble within 13. The ultimate goal is to match his haul of 13 league titles, five FA Cups, four League Cups and two Champions Leagues, alongside his other trophies.

5) The Graham Potter Challenge - Start in Sweden’s fourth tier and work your way up to managing a top-six Premier League club, following Graham Potter’s remarkable journey from Östersunds FK through Swansea City and Brighton to Chelsea.

6) The Godfather Challenge - Start at Palermo or Catania and choose a player under 20 with no senior international caps. Take him to every club you manage, even if it means following him after an unwanted sale. Your goal is to reach Serie A, win trophies together and turn your chosen player into an international star and major individual award winner.

7) The Stoke City/Bilbao Challenge - Take charge of Stoke City and adopt Athletic Bilbao's Basque-only transfer policy, but with a twist... you can only sign players from Staffordshire. Good luck.

8) The Brexit Challenge - Take charge of a proper Brexit club like Millwall. You can only sign British players with 14+ aggression, and you MUST play 4-4-2.

9) The A-Z of Football Challenge - Start unemployed with Sunday League experience and only apply for clubs beginning with A. Win a trophy, resign and move on to B, working your way through the alphabet. If you get sacked, you must stay on the same letter until you win a trophy.

10) The European Team in Africa Challenge: Take charge of AD Ceuta, a Spanish club based in North Africa, bordering Morocco. Starting in Spain's second division, can you take them to the top of Spanish football and bring the Champions League trophy to Africa?

11) Glory Hunter Challenge - We all want to be Jose Mourinho. Your aim in this challenge is to win the main division and domestic cup in each main European league. You also have to win the Champions League and Europa League.

12) Jay from the Inbetweeners Challenge - win the Champions League with Woking. 

13) The San Marino Challenge - Take charge of San Marino Calcio and guide them to Serie A. Reinvest your earnings into youth facilities, develop homegrown talent and use them to transform the San Marino national team, lifting them off the bottom of the FIFA rankings.

14) University Challenge - Win a continental competition with a university affiliated team. The UEFA options you have: Universitatea Craiova (Romania), Academica (Portugal), Queen's University (Northern Ireland), UCD (Republic of Ireland), Cardiff Met Uni or Swansea Uni (Wales)

15) The Journeyman With a Twist Challenge - Play a normal journeyman save, but you MUST accept every job offer you receive. About to win the Champions League but a League One club wants you? Tough, you're going. You also can't deliberately sabotage job interviews.

16) The Diego Simeone Challenge - Simulate La Liga until 6 November and take charge of whichever club sits 10th. Your goal is to break Real Madrid and Barcelona's dominance using ultra-defensive, aggressive tactics, just like Diego Simeone.

17) The Leonardo DiCaprio Challenge - You can only sign and play players under 25, and must sell them as soon as they turn 25. Your goal is to dominate world football with a squad that never gets too old for Leonardo DiCaprio.

18) The Watford Challenge  - Survive longer than a month at Watford 

19) The original Premier League Challenge - Get every original 1992/93 premier league back to the premier league. Once promoted, resign and find the next club to return to the premier league - Norwich, Blackburn, QPR, Sheff Wed, Wimbledon, Sheff United, Coventry, Ipswich, Oldham and Boro! Good luck!

20) The Hero to Zero Challenge - Take charge of a top-flight club and get them relegated all the way to the lowest playable division without getting sacked. You must survive every relegation, keep the board on your side and somehow convince them you're still the right man for the job. Potentially the hardest challenge in Football Manager.

21) Manage a team in the MLS. 

22) The Build a Nation Challenge - Take charge of a club in a smaller footballing nation and turn its domestic league into one of Europe's best. Win European trophies, improve your nation's UEFA coefficient and develop local talent, while strengthening rival clubs through transfers and loans. Your ultimate goal is to turn the entire league into a European powerhouse.

23) The Build a Nation From Abroad Challenge - Pick a country and manage a club outside it. Sign and develop players from your chosen nation while trying to win trophies with your club. Your ultimate goal is to improve that country's FIFA ranking and help them qualify for the World Cup without ever managing there or taking charge of their national team.

24) The Never-Ending Save Challenge - Start a normal save, but whenever you get bored, start a new challenge in the same game world instead of restarting. Keep going for decades or even centuries as football completely changes around you. Fallen giants, new superpowers, unexpected rivalries and endless rebuild opportunities. One save, unlimited challenges.

25) The Head Coach Challenge - Take charge of any club and delegate all transfers, contracts and scouting to your Director of Football. You can only manage tactics, training and matches, with no say in who gets signed or sold. Can you win trophies with a squad you have absolutely no control over building?

26) The Director of Football Challenge - Take charge of a club but act solely as its Director of Football. Control transfers, contracts, scouting and squad building while delegating all tactics, training and matches to your assistant manager. Your goal is to build a trophy-winning club without ever managing a match yourself.

27) The Last Dance Challenge - Build a trophy-winning team entirely around ageing footballers. You can only sign players aged 33 or older, and youth intake players cannot feature in your starting XI. The ultimate objective is to win domestic and continental silverware with a squad approaching retirement.

28) Hall of Fame Challenge - Build a managerial career with the ultimate goal of reaching No. 1 in Football Manager's worldwide Hall of Fame. Win domestic leagues, cups, continental and international trophies to accumulate points and overtake Sir Alex Ferguson as the greatest manager of all time.

29) The FC Vaduz Challenge - Take charge of Liechtenstein's FC Vaduz, who play in the Swiss league system but cannot qualify for Europe through their league position. Your only route is through the Liechtenstein Cup. Can you navigate your way from the Conference League to Champions League glory?

30) Youth Academy Only Challenge - Take charge of any club, but you're banned from signing players or bringing in loans. You can only use players already at the club and those coming through your youth intake. The ultimate goal is to win the Champions League with a completely homegrown squad.

31) The Beating the Big Brother Challenge - Take charge of a smaller club overshadowed by a giant rival in the same city, like Paris FC vs PSG or 1860 Munich vs Bayern. Your goal is to overtake them, win more trophies and become the biggest club in the city.

32) Into the Future Challenge - Simulate 5, 15 or even 50 years into the future before taking charge of a club. With new footballing superpowers, fallen giants and entirely new generations of players, the challenge is to build a successful career in a completely transformed football world.

33) The Proclaimers Challenge - Start at a club in Fife, Scotland, and guide them to the top division. Then move to clubs roughly 500 miles apart, winning a league title at each stop as you travel across the footballing world.

34) Build-a-league Challenge - Take charge of a club in a league outside Europe's traditional top five, such as Portugal or the Netherlands, and turn the entire league into a European powerhouse. Develop domestic talent, strengthen rival clubs and improve European performances, with the ultimate goal of taking your nation to No. 1 in the UEFA coefficient rankings.

35) The City Group Challenge - Embrace your inner villain and join the dark side of football by taking charge of clubs owned by the City Football Group. Win a league title with every club in the network, working your way towards Manchester City. The ultimate goal is to turn one of their smaller clubs into an even bigger footballing powerhouse than City themselves.

36) The Free Agent Challenge - Build a successful team without ever paying a transfer fee. You can only sign free agents, loan players or develop talent through your youth academy. The ultimate goal is to win major trophies without spending a penny on transfers.

37) The Tactic Rotation Challenge - Challenge yourself to master different tactical styles by changing your formation and playing philosophy every season, from 4-4-2 to tiki-taka or gegenpressing. For extra chaos, spin a wheel before every match to randomly decide which tactic you must use, regardless of your opposition.

38) Restore a Fallen Giant - Take charge of a historic club that has fallen from grace and return them to the top of European football. Options include Bordeaux (six-time French champions, now in the sixth tier), Real Zaragoza (European trophy winners, now in Spain's third tier), Sampdoria (1991 Serie A champions, now in Serie B) and Kaiserslautern (four-time German champions, now in the second tier). The ultimate goal is to restore their former glory and win major trophies again.

39) The Island-Hopping Challenge - Travel across Europe managing clubs based on different islands, such as Bastia (Corsica), Palermo (Sicily), Santa Clara (Azores), Tenerife (Canary Islands) and Tromso (Tromsøya). You can only manage clubs whose stadiums are physically located on an island, with no mainland clubs allowed. The ultimate goal is to win 10 top-flight league titles in 10 different countries, each with a club based on a different island.

40) The Record Breaker Challenge - Take charge of any club and attempt to break some of football's most iconic records. Concede fewer than the 15 goals Mourinho's Chelsea allowed in 2004/05, surpass Manchester City's 100-point Premier League season and chase Real Madrid's five consecutive European Cups. The ultimate goal is to rewrite the record books and build the greatest team football has ever seen.

41) The Invincibles Challenge - Take charge of any club and attempt to replicate Arsenal's legendary 2003/04 season by winning the league without losing a single match. For an extra challenge, go unbeaten in all competitions, including domestic cups and Europe, and complete an invincible treble.

42) The Manchester United Challenge - Your job is to sign one new defender for Man United and high press for one game. Impossible. 

43) The Snow White and the Seven Dwarves Challenge - Take charge of any club and build a successful team around unusually short players. You must start every match with at least ten under 5'8", with no exceptions. The ultimate goal is to win major trophies despite your obvious height disadvantage.

44) The Harry Redknapp Car Window Challenge - You're only allowed to sign players on transfer deadline day. You can scout all year, but every incoming transfer has to be completed on the final day of the window. Your aim is to win the Premier League while doing your entire summer's business in a few hours. Lovely player, top player, triffic.

45) The Revenge Recruitment Challenge - You're only allowed to sign players who have scored against you in your current save. Every striker who's ruined your weekend becomes a potential transfer target. Your goal is to win the Champions League with a squad built entirely from players who once made your life miserable.

46) The Zero Tolerance Challenge - Every time a player complains about playing time, contracts or wanting a transfer, you must immediately transfer-list them. No negotiations, no promises, no exceptions. Your goal is to win the Champions League while running the most unpleasant dressing room in Europe.

47) The Relegation Vultures Challenge - Take charge of a top-flight club, but you're only allowed to sign players from teams relegated at the end of the previous season. No poaching wonderkids from successful clubs. Build a title-winning squad entirely from players whose last campaign ended in absolute disaster.

48) The 007 Challenge - Become football's answer to James Bond. 0 league titles, 0 European trophies, 7 domestic cups. Your aim is to win seven cups across your career without ever winning a league title or European trophy. Being consistently brilliant and completely incapable of winning the league is harder than it sounds.

49) The Never Been to a World Cup Challenge - Take charge of any club, but you can only sign players representing nations that have never qualified for the men's World Cup. Your goal is to win the Champions League with a starting XI featuring 11 different nations that have never reached football's biggest tournament.

50) The Road to Wembley Challenge - Take charge of Wembley FC, an actual non-league club, and guide them to an FA Cup final at the stadium that shares their name. Better still, win the bloody thing. You'll need an expanded English lower-league database.

51) The Loan Sharks Challenge - You're banned from permanently signing anybody. Every new player must arrive on loan, with your academy filling the gaps. Your goal is to win a domestic title with a squad you effectively have to rebuild every summer. Choose your league carefully because loan restrictions could make this impossible.

52) The Tour de France Challenge - Pick one player and take him on a journey across France, bringing him with you every time you change clubs. At each stop, he must reach a target of 25 goals or assists before you can move on. The final destination is PSG, where your player must become a club legend and lead them to Champions League glory.

53) The UK Challenge - Manage in all four UK nations and break their single-season top-flight goalscoring records. Start in Northern Ireland (27 goals), then Scotland (35, Henrik Larsson), Wales (47) and finally England (60, Dixie Dean). You can use a different striker in each country, but must beat each target before moving on.

54) The Premier League Second Chances Challenge -  Your goal is to get every former Premier League club currently outside the top flight promoted back at least once. You don't have to manage them all. Use transfers, loans and financial boosts to help clubs like Oldham and Swindon return to the Premier League, even if you're managing elsewhere.

55) The British Steel Challenge - Travel across England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, attempting to win every domestic trophy available, from lower-league cups to top-flight titles. You can only use British and Irish players, forcing you to build entirely homegrown squads. The ultimate goal is to become the most decorated manager in British and Irish football history.

56) The Net Profit Challenge - Build a successful managerial career while always maintaining a positive net transfer spend. You can only buy players if your total transfer income exceeds your total transfer expenditure across your entire career. Every transfer must keep you in profit, with the ultimate goal of winning major trophies without ever spending more than you've earned from player sales.

57) The French Overseas Challenge - Take charge of a tiny club from a French overseas territory, like Club Franciscain (Martinique), AS Pirae (Tahiti) or CS Moulien (Guadeloupe). Your goal is to win the Coupe de France, overcoming professional French giants like PSG and Marseille despite having a fraction of their resources and travelling thousands of miles for away games.

58) The Extreme Pentagon Challenge - Start unemployed with no coaching badges or playing experience and win all five continental club competitions. The twist? You can only manage clubs from countries that have NEVER produced a winner of that continent's top club competition. Your goal is to make history on five continents.

59) The Lisbon Lions Challenge - Take charge of any club and win the league and Champions League using only players born in your club's country or holding its nationality. You must also include at least five academy graduates in every league match-day squad. For the ultimate challenge, only use players born within 30 miles of your stadium, just like Celtic's legendary Lisbon Lions.

60) The Get Me Home Challenge - Start your career in a footballing minnow far from home, such as Kosovo if you're from the UK. You can only move to clubs in neighbouring countries and must win a domestic trophy before crossing each border. Your ultimate goal is to work your way back home, with the extra challenge of managing in every country along your route.

61) The Race Across the World Challenge - Inspired by the BBC series, start unemployed with no coaching badges and travel from one country to another, aiming to reach a final destination via designated checkpoints. You can only move to neighbouring countries after winning a trophy, and must win a top-flight league or domestic cup at each checkpoint before continuing. The ultimate goal is to complete your journey across the world as quickly as possible.

62) The Area Challenge - Pick a region of the world, such as Scandinavia, the British Isles or the seven Arabian Peninsula states, and win the top-flight league title in every country. You can only move on after winning silverware. For an extra challenge, choose a region you know nothing about, like Central Asia or Central Africa.

63) The Shithouse Challenge - Inspired by the legendary Millwall Reddit save, take charge of any club and build the dirtiest, most aggressive team in football history. Sign players with high aggression, bravery and dirtiness, use hard tackling and aim to break records for fouls, yellow cards and red cards. The ultimate goal is to win major trophies while being the most ill-disciplined team in the league.

64) The Carlo Ancelotti Challenge - Start in Italy's Serie B (or lower) and replicate Ancelotti's legendary career. Win the league in all five major European nations (England, Spain, Italy, Germany and France), collect domestic cups and win at least six Champions Leagues to surpass his record of five. You must also win Manager of the Year in three different countries. Bonus challenge: Use 4-4-2 for at least one managerial spell.

65) The PokéPlayer Challenge - Gotta catch 'em all! Sign a player from every nationality available in Football Manager, with each playing at least 20 competitive matches for your club. Dual and triple nationalities count, there's no minimum playing time per appearance and no time limit. Your goal is to complete the ultimate footballing Pokédex.

66) The Retirement Home Challenge: Take charge of any club and build a squad entirely made up of players aged 30 or older. You can only sign players over 30, and anyone younger must be sold or released. The ultimate goal is to win major trophies with a team of ageing veterans, proving experience matters more than youth.

67) Neil Warnock challenge - try and get as many teams promoted in 20 years as possible.

68) The Passport Challenge - You're only allowed to manage clubs in cities you've visited in real life. Win a trophy in every country you've travelled to. If Real Madrid offer you a job but you've never been to Madrid, you're not allowed to accept it. A reason to book another holiday.

69) The Retired Shirt Numbers Challenge - Every time a player leaves your club, permanently retire their squad number. You can never use it again, even for a new signing. Try to win the Champions League before you run out of numbers and have to start handing out shirts with three digits.

70) The Phoenix Club Challenge - Take over a club formed after an older one collapsed, such as Union Brescia. Rebuild from scratch without relying on takeover money, reach the level the original club last played at and win a trophy its predecessor never managed.

71) The National Team Spine Challenge - Manage a club and a national team at the same time. You can only sign players eligible for that country, and your goal is to get at least 80% of the national squad playing for your club. Win the league and a major international tournament using your own players.

72) The Original Champions Challenge - Take over the first-ever winner of a major competition, such as Preston North End, who won the inaugural Football League in 1888/89. Recreate their historic triumph using only players eligible for the club's home nation. Five seasons to put the original champions back on top.

73) The One-Year Contract Challenge - Nobody at your club can sign a contract longer than one year. Each summer you're forced to negotiate with your entire squad or lose players for nothing. Can you build a title-winning side when your best players are permanently six months away from leaving?

74) The Forced Seller Challenge - Stay with one club for your entire managerial career, but accept every transfer offer that meets a player's valuation. You can never reject a fair offer, no matter how important the player. Win the Champions League while constantly losing your best footballers.

75) The Golden Boot Relay - Win the Golden Boot with a striker, then move to a new country and do it again with a different player. Repeat in five countries without ever signing a previous winner.

77) The Cup Giant-Killer Challenge - Start outside the top flight and win the domestic cup before earning promotion. You're not allowed to take a top-flight job or deliberately get promoted until the cup is won. Extra points if you knock out three top-flight clubs in the same run.

78) The Regicide Challenge - Take charge of a club in a league dominated by one team, such as Bayern Munich in Germany or PSG in France. Your goal is to end their dominance, win three consecutive league titles and establish a new dynasty.

Bears vs. Patriots is a tremendous primetime matchup highlighted by two high-end, young quarterbacks in Caleb Williams and Drake Maye

Along with a phenomenal coaching matchup in Ben Johnson’s Chicago offense vs. Mike Vrabel’s New England defense

With Josh McDaniels vs. Dennis Allen on the other side

Here’s some thoughts on Thursday Night Football
- First, Maye is in a significantly better position to succeed tonight than Williams, as the Bears have a much more exploitable defense than the Patriots.

- Maye is a killer when he’s comfortable, meaning he absolutely shreds teams in 7-on-7 type environments. Maye is fine when handling one rusher, things get messy for him when he sees stacked pressure, usually from high-end defenses. The difference between the two environments has been obvious for two years.

- Chicago is not a high-end defense, they are a group elevated by Allen, who is a plus play caller that has created a ton of margin over the last two years given what he has to work with.

- The Bears have a nearly non-existent four-man rush currently with edges Montez Sweat and Dayo Odeyingbo sidelined. That’s why Allen has been bringing heat via linebackers, safeties and even cornerbacks.

- McDaniels knows this. More passing game work for TreVeyon Henderson would make sense, but New England seems to have trust issues with Henderson, which certainly weren’t helped by his fumble last week. So, while that’s nice in theory, based on Henderson’s current workload in the passing game this season, a notable uptick would be a departure from what the Patriots do on offense, even if it would make a ton of sense if he started to see more targets to try to get him in space.

- Rhamondre Stevenson has less game breaking talent than Henderson, but the veteran is more reliable and well-rounded, especially against a team that is going to bring pressure at an above average rate on high leverage downs. Is Stevenson left in to block in these situations, or is he left in to block and then peel off? That’s a major question for me, and something I thought Atlanta really missed on last week with Bijan Robinson, I thought he should have seen a few screens and he should have been peeling off into the flat after some of his blocks.

- Next, Kyler Gordon is generally an excellent downhill nickel corner, and he’s coming off an outrageous week in that phase where he had 3 sacks and a number of pressures on a limited number of snaps against Atlanta. Another very interesting component of this matchup for me is 1. Does Gordon see a bump in playing time this week and 2. If so, I’d imagine DeMario Douglas sees most of the slot reps. Given how frequently Allen sent Gordon last week, and that Allen no doubt knows what Maye is when pressured versus when he’s not, making the route combinations New England deploys with Douglas (or whoever else is in the slot) with their running backs and Hunter Henry will be one of the keys to this game.

- I could see A.J. Brown’s game going a bit like Drake London’s last week, which is closer to solid despite strong volume than a monster output, as Brown is the guy you game plan for. Meaning linebackers drifting into slants on Brown’s side, over the top help, etc.

- I will, however, be curious to see if Brown sees more snaps in the slot this week, given Chicago’s willingness to blitz from the nickel. I’m also curious to see if he shows more, because dating back to last year he has not looked like the player he once was.

- I could also see Brown being put in motion often, both to make him harder to deal with and to help Maye with presnap reads, as identifying when Allen is bringing pressure, and from where, is the big solve tonight for Maye and New England.

- If Romeo Doubs was active I could see him having a very strong game here, but that puts Kyle Williams in an interesting position where I could see him landing at least one shot play in addition to some extra volume.

- If you’re the Bears, the two things I wouldn’t want to see are New England trying to get Henderson in space and Brown seeing an uptick in slot reps.

- The key to that side of this game is can Allen create enough pressure to give Maye issues, or can McDaniels/ New England’s pass protection put Maye in a position to not only succeed, but shred.

- On the other side of things, Ben Johnson isn’t easy to figure out but the strength of the Patriot’s defense is their corners and that, paired with Williams still coming off a hamstring injury, says to me more variants of two tight end personnel than 11.

- The Bears offensive line should be able to handle New England’s front, depending on how reduced right guard Jonah Jackson is while playing through hip and quadricep issues. Earlier in the week it was thought Jackson would miss this game, but he’s gritting it out. Since the strength of New England’s front is the interior, and the Bears have a tremendous guard duo, Jackson’s status, even though he’s playing, is a big one against this opponent.

- Vrabel’s defense in Tennessee and now in New England are both groups that I’d frame as they make things tight on the back end, meaning they force a lot of tight windows. Having seen what former Titans DC Shane Bowen did in New York without Vrabel last year, I have internalized this as a Vrabel thing.

- D’Andre Swift in space is interesting, as is Colston Loveland running across (or behind) New England’s linebacker level. Those strike me as the two best matchups for Chicago skill players.

- I’d imagine Rome Odunze sees a lot of Christian Gonzalez, and that’s a very tough matchup for Odunze.

- I could see Luther Burden having another game where he doesn’t see a huge snap share but when he’s on the field he sees a good target share, as he has a better matchup than Odunze.

- I noticed rookie speedster Zavion Thomas is starting to be worked in the offense last week. He does not need to run a full route tree to be useful, he can bring immediate value on slants, drags, screens and go routes. I don’t think Johnson will have him do anything complicated, especially not against this defense, but I could see a shot play and a screen for Thomas tonight.

- Overall, this is a coin flip type of game that I could see being around 40 total points, or one that gets past 60 given the quality of quarterbacks involved. Those tend to be my favorite island games.

- It would not surprise me if this ends up being the best Thursday Night Football game all year, especially if you’re a coaching enthusiast.

Here’s what I’m looking at on this slate

- Bijan Robinson should see 30 touches this week as 2-4 Atlanta is a live underdog against undefeated, but injury-reduced San Francisco.

He is, however, a very good defensive coordinator that is not only doing an excellent job in San Francisco so far, but he’s very familiar with Michael Penix. I’d expect pressure, where I’d sincerely hope Kevin Stefanski and his staff tries to catch the Niners with some screens and proactive checkdowns to Bijan, in an effort to get him in space.

- The 3-2 Lions are coming off their bye against a 4-2 Packers team that has played well during their three-game winning streak, but with Micah Parsons, Javon Hargrave and Edgerrin Cooper already on the shelf, the Packers are down linebacker Zaire Franklin as well. That’s not good when facing Detroit’s loaded offense, and especially not good when having to manage Jahmyr Gibbs without your best linebackers.

- One of the things that makes Detroit so difficult to deal with is if a defense overcommits to Gibbs, who is a killer in space and can break a run at any given time, they can hurt you with Jameson Williams over the top, Sam LaPorta in one-on-one matchups, and Amon-Ra St. Brown is among the league’s most reliable receivers, and he’s due for a bit of a blowup.

- Detroit has a good pass rush that will have a trench advantage in this matchup, but their secondary has been atrocious. Safety Brian Branch looks like he’ll return this week, which is an obvious plus. Given Green Bay’s speedsters in Christian Watson and Matthew Golden (who has an injury uncertainty) Detroit just about has to play two high or cover 4 at a high rate, with light boxes, basically inviting Green Bay to run and win via a death by a thousand cuts type of offensive approach.

- Josh Jacobs returns, and a quick passing game could help Jordan Love and Green Bay’s patch work offensive line (which has played well considering) mitigate Detroit’s front.

- Love historically plays efficiently against Detroit, but he’s never thrown for more than 273 yards against the Lions, and he’s only gone for more than 250 twice in his career against Detroit.

- The line in Ravens vs. Bengals has moved back and forth throughout the week, as Lamar Jackson’s status for this contest is still up in the air.

- If Jackson plays, his Ravens vs. Joe Burrow’s Bengals is one of, if not the best intra-division quarterback matchup in the entire league.

- If he doesn’t, outgunning Burrow is a super tall order for Tyler Huntley.

- Over the past two years Ja’Marr Chase has gone for over 100 yards in each of his last four matchups against Baltimore, with at least 10 receptions in three of those four contests

- The Bengals have a one-dimensional offense, as Chase Brown is a very average player, so Cincinnati should be in the market for a cost-effective upgrade at running back.

- After Cam Skattebo did not see a carry last week, I would be surprised if that happened again in Houston, especially since New York will no doubt use their running game to try and slow down the Texan’s high-end edge duo. It would also make sense, given who coaches this team, if Devin Singletary saw more work than Tyrone Tracy given the quality of Houston’s pass rush. Singletary isn’t a very interesting skill player, but John Harbaugh and his staff no doubt trusts him more than Tracy in pass protection and similar areas.

- Abdul Carter is game planned for every week where he sees a lot of doubles and help, but if the Giants are going to have any kind of shot here, he needs to make a few plays to get the Giants off the field. Similarly, Kayvon Thibodeaux is the kind of former first round edge you do not pay big money to, because he feasts on bad offensive tackles, which he isn’t even doing this year as he’s still in search for his first sack. However, I’m mentioning this because Houston is the sort of offensive line Thibodeaux tends to have a spike game against, historically.

- The Jets have a better roster than Miami, where I’d argue New York is better at every position group but linebacker, and even that is close. That said, coming off their bye, this might be the Dolphins best shot to win a game all year, with the caveat that I do genuinely think they could go winless.

- If the Dolphins win this game, I’d expect that Jeff Hafley and his staff will create some strategic margin coming off their bye, particularly by pressuring Smith.

That said, two weeks ago on Thursday Night Football I thought Buccaneers perimeter corners did an excellent job on CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, who I’d call “bigs” for this purpose as they are similar to Carolina’s wide receiver duo in that sense.

That’s the one downside in Mayfield’s matchup as his offensive line should mitigate Carolina’s push while the Panthers are down their best edge and both of their perimeter corners. Tampa is also in a desperation spot at 1-5, where a loss just about buries them, but a win keeps them much closer to alive in football’s second messiest division.

- The Vikings are coming off their bye and the idea of Brian Flores against Daniel Jones is almost hilarious to me (Jones is one of the few players in the league that I’d call myself a hater of). That said, the Colts firing their general manager strikes me as more of a warning shot to the rest of the roster than a white flag.

- The Colts could realistically string together a good defensive effort and they have a good enough offensive line to at least somewhat mitigate Flores’ pressure packages, but ultimately Jones is the liability in this matchup.

- I thought the Colts could be scrappy this season behind a high-end run game and a good defense, but this game in Minnesota could end up being a last stand of sorts for Indianapolis this season.

- Arizona is coming off a banner win and therefore a classic letdown spot for a volatile team like they are while the Broncos are coming off a long week with trench advantages on both sides of the ball. Denver will be without stud safety Talanoa Hufanga, with star corner back Patrick Surtain currently listed as questionable.

- This seems like a good matchup to try to get Bo Nix and Jaylen Waddle going with some early manufactured touches. A throw early to run light type of approach would make sense both for this specific game, and for Sean Payton’s need to get more out of Nix over the long haul.

- The Steelers have a trench advantage against New Orlean’s injury reduced offensive line, while Pittsburgh is coming off a near full overtime period last week. That overtime component mixed with this game being in Paris is why I can’t quite say that I’d be surprised if the Steelers lost, as those are two unwanted variables that gum up the works, so to speak.

- Germie Bernard has served as an underneath, pretty high-volume option for Aaron Rodgers in each of the last two games. Think of him as Rodgers’ Cole Beasley currently.

- This is a must win game for the spiraling, injury ravaged Rams whose pass catcher group will be a genuine nightmare if Puka Nacua is sidelined. Even if Puka played, expect a great deal of 12 and 13 personnel (tight end heavy) out of the Rams.

- Given those constraints, it would be no real surprise if this was an abnormally running back centric game plan from Sean McVay.

- The Rams defensive front is down multiple starters, so if Ashton Jeanty is going to see any rushing lanes this season, this looks like a good opportunity against the Rams.

- It was genuinely hard to watch Eagles quarterback Tanner McKee last week, as he is very limited in pressure management. If the Cowboys can’t limit this Eagles’ offense, who are down two of their three best opening day linemen, with virtually every one of their starting skill position players on the injury report, heads need to roll in Dallas given the stakes of this game.

- Despite Philadelphia’s offensive struggles, Vic Fangio’s defense has kept the Eagles in each of the last three games, even though they were losses.

- I have never been a big Dak Prescott guy, he’s the definition of a hall of good quarterback that you’re going to need to give an all-star team to have any shot at being a contender. This Cowboys team is not an all-star team.

- I’d pin a good chunk of the Cowboys losses to the Buccaneers and Packers on Prescott. If he plays like he did in those two outings, Dallas could lose on Monday night.

- Seahawks vs. Chiefs is a really interesting game as you get to see Mike Macdonald’s aggressive pressure packages not only against Patrick Mahomes, who is among the very best at managing difficult pressure, but against former Seahawks running back Kenneth Walker. That’s a true marquee bout.

- Speaking of pressure, pressure rate and things of that nature are extremely incomplete stats. The next time you watch a football game, pay attention to the wide range there is for the pressure a team generates. Against a guy like Mahomes, he’ll often evade one rusher, he’ll even evade a stacked, second rusher more often than just about anyone, but the difference between those two types of pressure are enormous, as one creates moderate stress while the second, stacked version is the primary way defenses can derail games, and Seattle is one of the best at creating those situations where multiple players are creating impactful pressure. So, when someone gives me a stat like pressure rate, this is why I don’t care, as it’s a very incomplete accounting of events where I’m basically being given a shittier version of batting average. It’s not completely useless, but it’s hardly telling me the whole story.

- I am very, very curious to see what Steve Spagnuolo does to try and limit Jaxon Smith-Njigba. In general I could see Spagnuolo’s defense stealing this game, but whether or not he does anything very creative to try and limit JSN in high leverage spots is of great interest to me.

I have watched every NFL game for roughly a decade. I have done this for the purpose of sports speculation.

I run a reality-based program here.

Engagement is how I reach new users. So as long as engagement remains strong (comments/ shares) I’ll continue pumping this and similarly detailed insights out every week.

This rock looked like nothing. That is the only reason it deserves the next two and a half minutes of your life.

Not a gemstone. Not a meteorite. Not a relic with a legend stapled to it. Just a lump of weathered stone lying where lumps of weathered stone have always lain, the kind of object your eye slides past a hundred times a day without ever filing it. Nobody walks up to a rock like that expecting to be rewarded.

And yet, in the way it is handled, you can tell that somebody is expecting exactly that.

I keep returning to that gap. The distance between what a thing looks like and what a thing is. It is the oldest tension in the world, older than money, older than language, and this clip is built entirely on top of it. I am not going to tell you what happens in it. I am going to tell you why it is engineered to work on you, why the human mind cannot leave a closed object alone, and why the last two words of the title, "AI Reveal," may be the most interesting part of the whole thing.

Because here is the uncomfortable question underneath all of it: if a rock can look like nothing and hold something, can a video look like proof and hold nothing?

Hold that thought. We will come back to it.

First, the rock.

THE PROBLEM WITH ORDINARY

Ordinary is a survival feature. Your brain has to process an absurd amount of visual noise every waking second, and to cope it runs a ruthless filter: anything that looks like background gets demoted to background. Gravel. Bark. Pavement. Stones. They are not rejected so much as never admitted. You could walk the same dirt path for ten years and be unable to describe a single stone on it.

That filter is efficient, and it is also exactly where treasure hides. Not in vaults. Not under dramatic cliffs marked with an X. In the category of things you have already decided not to look at.

Every great discovery story has a moment where somebody refused the filter. Someone picked up the thing everyone else stepped over. Someone asked a question that sounded foolish because the object did not look like it deserved a question. The story is rarely "he found something amazing." It is almost always "he paid attention to something that looked unworthy of attention," and the amazing part came afterward, as a consequence.

That is the first reason this clip lands. It does not begin with a prize. It begins with a refusal to dismiss.

THE MOST POWERFUL EMOTION YOU CAN FEEL ABOUT A CLOSED OBJECT

In 1994, the behavioral economist George Loewenstein published a paper proposing what is now called the information gap theory of curiosity. The idea is simple and slightly brutal. Curiosity is not a love of knowledge. It is a kind of discomfort, triggered when you become aware of a specific gap between what you know and what you want to know. The wider the gap feels, and the closer you are to closing it, the more it itches.

Notice the two conditions. You must know enough to realize something is missing. And you must believe the answer is within reach.

A closed rock satisfies both with almost insulting efficiency. You know it has an inside. You know the inside exists right now, this very second, whether or not you ever see it. The answer is not in the future or in another country. It is physically present, a few centimeters of stone away, and the only thing standing between you and the truth is a barrier you can see with your own eyes.

Compare that with almost any other mystery. A locked door tells you a room exists. A sealed envelope tells you words exist. But a rock offers something stranger: it is the only closed container that was never designed to contain anything. Nobody packed it. Nobody sealed it. Whatever is inside, if anything is, got there on its own, over a span of time that makes human history look like a blink.

So the question is not "what did someone hide?" The question is "what did the universe leave, and did anyone ever bother to check?"

That is a much bigger itch.

WHY YOUR BRAIN STARTS THE REWARD BEFORE THE REWARD

There is a second mechanism, and it is the one content creators understand intuitively even if they could never name it. Research on the brain's reward circuitry has repeatedly found that dopamine activity is tied less to receiving a reward than to predicting one. The pleasure is strongest in the leaning forward. In the moment where the outcome is possible but not yet known.

Slot machines are built on this. So are unwrapped presents, scratch cards, the last page of a thriller, and the half second after a penalty kick leaves the ball but before the keeper moves. What you are feeling in those moments is not the outcome. It is suspense itself, and suspense is, chemically speaking, a surprisingly rewarding state.

Which means the sealed rock is more potent than whatever is inside it. The unopened version carries every possible outcome at once. It is simultaneously a plain stone, a hollow, a vein, a surprise. The instant it opens, all of those futures collapse into one, and no matter how good that one is, something is lost. The possibility is over.

This is why reveal videos have become one of the most dependable formats on the internet. They do not sell outcomes. They sell the lean forward.

And I want to be honest about something: this post is doing exactly the same thing to you right now. It is a closed rock too. Every paragraph is a small chisel. The whole structure runs on the same machinery I am describing, and I would rather tell you that than pretend to be neutral. If you have read this far, you are already leaning.

Now let us talk about what rocks actually do.

WHAT A STONE CAN ACTUALLY HIDE

Here is the part that makes the fantasy less of a fantasy.

Rocks really do have insides that do not match their outsides. Geologists have a word for the most famous example: a geode. In the simplest terms, it is a rock with a cavity, and the cavity is lined with crystals. Some form when gas bubbles get trapped in cooling volcanic rock. Others begin as hollows in sedimentary layers. Then mineral-rich water finds its way in, slowly, and leaves its cargo behind on the walls, a microscopic layer at a time. Do that for a span of time measured in thousands of years, sometimes far more, and you get a chamber of crystals sealed inside a plain, dull shell.

Think about how strange that is. The outside of the stone is shaped by weather, abrasion, rain, rivers, the slow violence of ordinary erosion. The inside is shaped by stillness. One side of the same object has been battered by the world for ages. The other side has been growing in complete darkness, undisturbed, for just as long, and has never once been seen by anyone.

Two histories, one object, separated by a few centimeters of rind.

And the rind is not an accident. The hard outer layer is often precisely why the cavity survived at all. Soft surroundings wear away. The tough shell is what lets the quiet interior exist long enough to be found. The ugly part is the protection. The dull exterior and the hidden interior are not opposites. They are collaborators.

THE LARGEST SECRETS EVER OPENED

If this sounds like a small-scale curiosity, look at the extreme end of the scale.

In 1999, collectors exploring an abandoned mine near the town of Pulpi in southern Spain found a cavity lined with enormous gypsum crystals, large enough that people can actually climb inside it. Picture that. Not a rock you hold in your hands. A geode you walk into. It had sat sealed for ages, and nobody had known, because from the outside it was simply more mountain.

Then there is Naica, in Mexico. In 2000, miners drilling in a deep silver and lead mine broke into a chamber filled with selenite crystals the size of tree trunks, some of them many meters long. The air in there was so hot and so humid that a person without protective gear could last only minutes before the body began to fail. Beauty on a scale that was actively trying to kill anyone who came to look at it.

Both of those places sat in the dark for an unimaginable stretch of time. Both were found by people who happened to be in the wrong place and kept their eyes open. Neither announced itself.

Time is the silent co-author of every one of these places. It never hurries, it never advertises, and it does not care whether anyone ever arrives to appreciate the work, which may be the most humbling thing about it.

I am not saying any of that is what you will see in this clip. I am saying that the idea the clip plays with, ordinary exterior and extraordinary interior, is not a trick of the internet. It is a real property of the planet. The earth does this. The fantasy is built on a fact.

That is why it works. The fantasy never has to ask you to believe in something impossible. It only asks you to believe in something rare.

THE LOTTERY NOBODY TELLS YOU ABOUT

Now for the cold water, because a story without it is a brochure.

Most rocks are exactly what they look like. Solid, plain, ordinary all the way through. Split a hundred of them and the overwhelming majority will give you a clean gray face and nothing else. Even among stones that are hollow, a great many hold only a thin, unremarkable coat of common mineral. The spectacular ones are the exceptions, and the exceptions are the only ones that ever make it into a video.

This is a quiet form of selection bias, and it quietly rewrites how we feel about discovery. You see the stone that opened to something dazzling. You never see the forty that opened to nothing, because nobody films nothing. So the world starts to feel like a place where every plain-looking rock is secretly an opportunity, when the truth is closer to the opposite: the plain-looking rock is almost always just plain.

And still people go looking. Still they weigh stones in their palms. Still they tap them, listen for a hollow note, turn them over in the light, run a thumb across the surface searching for the faint seam, the small crack, any sign of a door.

Why? If the odds are that poor, why bother?

Because the cost of checking is small and the cost of never checking is invisible. You can recover from a wasted afternoon. You can never recover from the afternoon you walked past the thing and never knew. The second loss does not feel like a loss. It does not feel like anything. That is exactly what makes it dangerous.

THE IRREVERSIBLE PART

There is one more detail about opening a stone that I cannot stop thinking about.

You cannot undo it.

Every other kind of looking is free. You can glance at a painting, glance away, glance back. You can read a letter twice. A stone does not work like that. The only way to see inside is to break it, and a broken rock does not go back together. The act of discovering is the act of destroying the sealed version forever. The unopened stone, the one that held every possibility, gets sacrificed so that one possibility can exist.

So there is always a quiet moment before the break that feels, if you pay attention to it, strangely close to grief. A tiny funeral for the unknown. Whatever the outcome, wonderful or empty, the version of the world in which it could have been anything is finished.

People who handle rocks professionally talk about this in oddly gentle terms. Care. Patience. Reading the stone. They know the first strike is the one you cannot take back. They do not rush, because the stone has waited far longer than you have, and its schedule does not care about yours.

That patience is the real subject, hiding behind the spectacle. The thing worth noticing in this clip, the thing I would want you to watch for, is not the outcome. It is the fact that someone stayed with a stubborn object long enough for it to change. Most of what we call luck is just stubbornness that happened to be pointed in the right direction.

THE COLOR THAT HAS FOOLED EVERYONE

Now let us talk about the word in the title that makes everyone's pulse jump. Golden.

Humans respond to that color with a reflex older than any civilization. Warm, bright, heavy-looking, it signals value before a single thought has formed. It is also, and this is the part that should make you slow down, one of the most imitated looks in nature.

Geologists have a nickname for a whole family of glittering minerals that pass as the real thing at first glance: fool's gold. The best-known culprit is pyrite, a compound of iron and sulfur whose name comes from a Greek word for fire, because it throws sparks when struck against steel. It forms in crisp, geometric shapes, cubes and many-sided forms with sharp faces, and it shines with a brassy yellow that has embarrassed generations of hopeful people.

Real gold has a personality of its own. It is extraordinarily dense, far heavier than the lookalikes. It is soft enough to dent and scratch. It does not behave the way a brittle, sparkling mineral behaves. Experienced prospectors can often feel the difference in the hand before they ever reach for a test. But the first glance, the one that happens in the half second before experience kicks in, belongs entirely to the color. And the color lies.

History is full of the damage. In 1607, the first settlers at Jamestown became so convinced that glittering dirt was gold that they spent precious time and effort loading it onto a ship bound for England, while the colony itself was struggling to survive. In the 1570s, an English expedition led by Martin Frobisher hauled shiploads of dark ore home from the Arctic in the belief that it held a fortune, only for the cargo to prove essentially worthless.

Smart people. Serious expeditions. Real money. All undone by a shimmer.

I want you to hold onto that, because it changes how you should watch anything that glitters. The lesson of fool's gold is not that treasure is fake. It is that our desire to see treasure is stronger than our ability to examine it. We do not look at the glitter and then decide. We decide, and then we look.

I am not telling you that what appears in this clip is any of those things. I am telling you that the moment a golden shine enters a story, the viewer's honesty is the first thing to leave the room.

THE HAND THAT IS NOT ALLOWED TO HURRY

Let me say something about the people in stories like this, because they are the part we skip.

It is easy to imagine that discoveries come to the lucky. But watch how people who actually work with stone behave around it, and you notice a kind of discipline that has nothing to do with luck. They are slow when slowness is required. They stop. They tilt the object to catch the light. They test the weak points. They hesitate at precisely the moments when an amateur would swing harder.

Hesitation, here, is not fear. It is respect for irreversibility. It is the understanding that you get one clean attempt at something that took the planet an age to make.

There is also the sound. Anyone who has handled stone for long will tell you that the ears get involved before the eyes do. A solid piece rings differently from one with a void inside it, and a sealed hollow gives back a note that a dense lump never will. It is a primitive kind of sonar, learned entirely by repetition and passed from hand to hand, and it comes with no manual. Which is another small proof that the best knowledge about hidden things is rarely written down. It lives in the fingers and the ear, built from hundreds of ordinary failures that nobody ever filmed.

There is a lesson in that which has nothing to do with rocks. We live in an attention economy that rewards speed: the quick reaction, the instant verdict, the swipe. Almost everything worth finding in this world is behind a surface that punishes speed. A stone does not open faster because you are impatient. A person does not reveal themselves because you demanded it. A skill does not arrive because you wanted it today.

So when you watch someone work patiently on something unpromising, you are not only watching a task. You are watching a counterargument to the whole speed of modern life.

And that, I suspect, is a big part of why these clips travel. People do not only share the shiny outcome. They share the feeling of watching somebody refuse to rush.

WHY THIS FORMAT NEVER DIES

Step back and notice how many versions of this story the internet has told. The opened geode. The sealed crate in an abandoned storage unit. The pearl in the oyster. The painting under another painting. The old coin in the muddy field. The mystery box nobody has unwrapped yet.

They are all the same story wearing different costumes. A plain exterior. A promise. A barrier. A moment. A reveal.

The format survives because it matches something very deep in how we are wired. Every culture has told some version of it. The fairy tale about the beggar who is really a king. The humble village with the hidden spring. The ugly lamp with the genie inside. The universal fantasy is not wealth. It is recognition: the belief that value can exist unseen, that the overlooked may not be what it seems, that being dismissed is not the same as being worthless.

That is an enormously consoling idea. And it is why I think a rock can carry real emotion. Because underneath the sparkle, it is a story about being underestimated, told through an object that cannot be offended by it.

There is a mild irony in that. We are most moved by the idea of hidden worth when it belongs to something that cannot feel overlooked. A stone has no ego to bruise. We project it all ourselves. The emotion in these videos is not in the rock. It is in the viewer, borrowing the rock to say something about their own life.

So when you feel something watching a stone get opened, do not be embarrassed by it. You are not reacting to the stone. You are reacting to the possibility that the things you have written off, in the world and maybe in yourself, are not finished telling you what they hold.

THE TWO WORDS AT THE END OF THE TITLE

Now back to the thought I asked you to hold.

"AI Reveal."

Those two words quietly rewrite the contract between you and the video. Without them, you would be watching a reveal and judging only the outcome. With them, you are watching a reveal and judging the medium. The question stops being "what is inside the stone?" and becomes "what am I actually being shown, and by what?"

I will not pretend to know the answer for you, and I will not claim a verdict the title does not give. What I can say is that we have entered a period in which the sentence "I saw it with my own eyes" has lost most of its legal weight. Images can be made that never touched a camera. Footage can be assembled that never touched the world. And the most dangerous version of this is not the obviously fake clip. It is the one that is almost certainly believable, built from just enough reality that your suspicion has nowhere to land.

Here is the strange twist: the reveal genre is the perfect home for this tension. A reveal is, by design, a moment where the audience is told to stop analyzing and start feeling. Suspense switches off the critic. The better the buildup, the less likely you are to audit the payoff. Which means the format that has always been good at making people feel is now also the format best positioned to make people believe.

So perhaps the most honest way to watch something labeled this way is to hold two attitudes at once. Let yourself enjoy it. And keep a small, quiet investigator in the back row, taking notes.

HOW TO WATCH LIKE SOMEONE WHO CANNOT BE EASILY FOOLED

You do not need special software. You need four habits.

First, ask whether the inside belongs to the outside. Real objects carry their histories on their skins. A rock that has weathered for ages should tell a coherent story from rind to core. When the interior feels like it comes from a different universe than the exterior, that is not proof of anything, but it is worth noticing, and worth asking why.

Second, watch the light. Light is brutally hard to fake consistently. Crystals scatter it, bend it, throw it in multiple directions at once. Real mineral surfaces catch light unevenly, with chaos and glitches and dull patches next to bright ones. Perfect, even brilliance should always raise one eyebrow, not two.

Third, look for imperfection. Nature is untidy. Real crystal growth is crowded, interrupted, cluttered with flaws, broken edges, dust, and stains. If something feels as if it were arranged for display, ask who arranged it.

Fourth, and this one is the hardest, notice your own wanting. The strongest tool for deceiving anyone is the viewer's desire for the story to be true. The moment you catch yourself rooting for a particular outcome, you have just identified the weak point in your own judgment.

None of this requires cynicism. Skeptics are not the people who refuse to be amazed. They are the people who insist on being amazed accurately.

WHY IT MATTERS EVEN IF IT IS JUST A ROCK

You might be thinking: it is a video of a rock. Why are we doing all this?

Because the habits you practice on small things are the ones you carry into big things. If you can learn to enjoy a reveal while still asking where it came from, you are building a muscle you will need for every headline, every clip, every confident voice that arrives in your feed promising to show you the truth.

A harmless piece of content is a perfect training ground precisely because the stakes are low. Nobody is hurt when you misjudge a stone. So you can afford to examine your own reactions. When did you feel certain? What made you certain? Was it evidence, or was it music, timing, golden light, and a well-placed pause?

Those are not trivial questions. They are the questions that separate a person who consumes media from a person who is quietly consumed by it.

And there is a flip side that deserves equal weight. Skepticism that becomes automatic is its own kind of blindness. The person who assumes everything is fake will miss every real wonder the same way the person who assumes everything is real will miss every deception. The goal is not suspicion. The goal is attention. Real, patient, slightly stubborn attention, the same kind it takes to read a stone.

THE TWO ENDINGS

I have been circling this for a while, so let me say it plainly.

There are two possible stories hiding inside this clip, and both of them are worth your time.

In the first, the stone is what the stone appears to be, and the interior holds something that rewards the effort. Then you are watching a small, real instance of an enormous fact: that the earth keeps secrets in unremarkable packaging, and that the only way to learn them is to take the packaging seriously.

In the second, what you see is something engineered to feel exactly like the first story. Then you are watching something just as interesting: a demonstration of how easily the feeling of discovery can be manufactured, and how little it takes to make an audience gasp at something that never existed.

Either way, you come away knowing something. One version teaches you about the world. The other teaches you about yourself.

Which one it is, I am leaving for you to see.

WHAT I WOULD ACTUALLY TAKE FROM THIS

Strip away the sparkle, the suspense, the question of what is real, and one small, stubborn idea remains.

Nothing announces its own value. The valuable thing and the worthless thing often wear the same gray coat. The only difference between the people who find something and the people who walk past is a thin habit of attention: a willingness to stop, to wonder, to risk looking a little ridiculous in front of a plain object that gives no sign of deserving it.

That habit costs almost nothing. It is available to anyone. It does not require money, training, or luck. Only the small decision, repeated, to treat the unremarkable as unfinished.

I think that is why a short clip about a rock can follow you around afterward. It is not about stone. It is about how much of life is decided by whether you bother to look closely at the things that do not look like they matter.

So here is the invitation, and it is a real one, not a trick.

Watch it once for the feeling. Let your pulse do what it wants to do. Let the lean forward happen, because it is one of the better things a human nervous system can do on an ordinary afternoon.

Then watch it again for the evidence. Ask where the light goes. Ask whether the inside belongs to the outside. Ask what you wanted to be true, and how much that wanting did the seeing for you.

And when you have decided what you think, tell somebody. Send it to the friend who always says everything online is fake, and to the friend who believes all of it. Watch what each of them notices. The difference between their answers will tell you more than the clip will.

One last thing.

Somewhere right now there is another stone sitting in the dirt, waiting, in no hurry at all. It has been there longer than any of us have been alive. It does not care whether you look at it.

But you might.
